title: Jonah and the Garden
premise: Tamsin Thornbury has survived by being unremarkable: a smuggler's guide who speaks to beasts only when no one can hear, in the mountain country of Thornfell where her gift was outlawed a generation ago. When the crown's beast-hunters arrive with a relic that forces hidden speakers to answer its call, Tamsin's secret companions—a blind wolf, a scarred hawk, a half-tame wyrmling—begin answering for her, and her invisibility shatters. Hunted alongside a disgraced royal cartographer and a child whose own gift has already been discovered, she must reach the Verdant Door, the last passage out of Thornfell before the kingdom's borders are sealed and every speaker is conscripted or killed. But the Door demands a price: it opens only for one who surrenders what they most hide, and Tamsin must choose between erasing her gift to save herself, or claiming it fully—becoming the voice the hunted beasts have been waiting for. She chooses the gift, the Door remakes her into something neither fully woman nor fully wild, and the story ends not with escape but with a reckoning: Tamsin leading the mountain's creatures and the last free speakers back down to face the crown.
about_author: August Blackwood is the pen name of a former trail guide who spent six years mapping remote passes and claims the mountains taught them everything they know about silence. They write fantasy about people who belong to places more than they belong to people.

chapters.title: The Smuggler's Ledger
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She guides a smuggler's caravan through the Thornfell passes, quietly bargaining with a mountain goat herd to avoid a rockslide, and we see the double life she leads: flawless guide by day, whisperer to beasts in the dark. The beat is competence hiding loneliness.

chapters.title: What the Wolf Remembered
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A blind old wolf she's fed for years arrives at her cabin with a warning carried in images, not words: men in crown colors moving up the valleys with a caged thing that screams. She dismisses it as fear, but packs her go-bag anyway. The beat is dread she refuses to name.

chapters.title: The Proclamation at Millbrook
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, in town. The crown's herald reads the Edict of the Quiet Tongue: beast-speaking is treason, and a relic called the Hollow Bell will be rung in every market square to force speakers into revealing themselves. Tamsin watches a neighbor's dog answer the Bell—and the neighbor taken. The beat is terror in a crowd that must not show on her face.

chapters.title: The Bell's First Song
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. On the road home, a hunting party rings a portable Hollow Bell, and every animal within miles turns toward it—except Tamsin, who fights the pull by biting through her own lip. She realizes the Bell doesn't detect speakers; it enslaves beasts to betray them. The beat is the cost of silence: blood in her mouth.

chapters.title: The Cartographer's Debt
chapters.summary: Wren Alcott's POV. Wren, a royal cartographer imprisoned for falsifying border maps to hide refugee routes, escapes his escort during a rockslide Tamsin engineered. He finds her cabin and offers her something she can't refuse: he knows where the Verdant Door is. The beat is wary alliance between two people who lie professionally.

chapters.title: The Girl in the Hollow
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Following Wren's map, they find a feral child, Pip, hiding in a cave with a fox that speaks for her—Pip is a speaker too young to know how to stop. Tamsin, who has spent her life hiding, must decide whether to teach a child to hide or to be brave. The beat is reluctant tenderness.

chapters.title: Hollow Bell Rising
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The hunting party's commander, Serah Vane, is revealed: a former speaker who surrendered her gift to save her family and now hunts her own kind. Wren, captured briefly, learns Vane isn't cruel—she's convinced the Bell can be used to protect speakers by controlling them. The beat is an enemy with a reasonable, terrible logic.

chapters.title: The Wyrmling's Bargain
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A half-tame wyrmling, wounded by the Bell, blocks their pass and demands in broken speech a debt Tamsin's grandmother owed it: safe passage in exchange for the truth of the Door. The wyrmling reveals the Door opens only for one who surrenders their deepest secret. The beat is the first hint the escape has a price.

chapters.title: Ash on the Shepherd's Road
chapters.summary: Pip's POV. Pip witnesses a burned village where speakers were rooted out by their own livestock, and understands for the first time what being found means. Tamsin teaches her the first rule: the beasts are not witnesses, they are family. The beat is a child's innocence meeting atrocity, and choosing loyalty over fear.

chapters.title: The Pass That No Longer Exists
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren confesses his maps are wrong—the Verdant Door lies beyond a pass he erased from royal records, and only Tamsin's grandmother's smuggler's ledger can find it. But the ledger is in the crown's archive at Thornhold. The beat is the plan turning desperate: they must break into the fortress.

chapters.title: Thornhold by Night
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Using the Bell's own logic—beasts move freely where speakers cannot—Tamsin sends rats, owls, and the blind wolf to retrieve the ledger while she walks in as a captured speaker, bait for Vane. The beat is audacity, and the first time Tamsin uses her gift as a weapon rather than a secret.

chapters.title: Two Voices in a Cell
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane interrogates Tamsin and finds a mirror: a woman who hid her gift to survive, now watching another woman surrender hers to survive. Tamsin's argument—that the Bell doesn't protect speakers, it erases them—plants the first crack in Vane's certainty. The beat is the enemy beginning to doubt.

chapters.title: The Ledger and the Lie
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The wolf delivers the ledger, but the escape route through Thornhold collapses, and Wren is gravely wounded covering the retreat. Tamsin realizes the Door's price may demand exactly this kind of sacrifice, and refuses to let it. The beat is found family solidifying into something worth dying for.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Buried
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The ledger reveals her grandmother was not a smuggler but the Door's last Keeper, and that the 'surrender' it demands is not a secret given up but a self given up—speakers who enter are remade. Tamsin has been walking her grandmother's path all along. The beat is inheritance as both gift and trap.

chapters.title: Vane's Choice
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Ordered to ring the great Hollow Bell at the mountain's heart—which would enslave every beast in Thornfell permanently—Vane instead frees the wyrmling and defects, hunted now by her own soldiers. The beat is redemption earned, not granted, and it costs her everything she had left.

chapters.title: The Hunt on the High Snows
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The crown's full force pursues them up the glacier road; the blind wolf dies holding the pass, and Tamsin, grieving, stops running. She rings no Bell, but calls every free creature of Thornfell by name. The beat is grief transmuted into command.

chapters.title: The Verdant Door
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They reach the Door: a living arch of root and light that asks its price. Pip, Wren, and Vane can pass freely—but Tamsin must surrender what she most hides, and what she most hides is that she wants to belong to the wild more than to people. The beat is the choice the whole book has aimed at.

chapters.title: Remade
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin steps through and the Door remakes her: she can still speak to beasts, but now they hear her always, and she hears the land itself—a voice no longer hidden, no longer fully human. She returns through the Door changed, and Pip barely recognizes her. The beat is transcendence shadowed by loss.

chapters.title: The Kingdom That No Longer Exists
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Beyond the Door lies not freedom but a dead land—the other side of Thornfell was emptied generations ago; there was never anywhere to escape to. The Door was never an exit. It was a threshold, and someone had to cross it and come back. The beat is the collapse of the escape fantasy.

chapters.title: The Voice of Thornfell
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin leads the beasts and the last free speakers back down the mountain toward Thornhold, Vane at her side carrying the broken Hollow Bell as proof, Pip's fox carrying the child's message to every village: you are not alone, and hiding is over. The beat is the found family becoming a movement.

chapters.title: The Reckoning at Thornhold
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At the fortress gates, Tamsin speaks with the unified voice of Thornfell's creatures, and the land itself answers—rivers shift, roads close, the crown's soldiers find the mountain no longer theirs. The Bell is unmade. The beat is the climax: not a battle won by force, but by a voice that cannot be silenced.

chapters.title: Jonah and the Garden
chapters.summary: Pip's POV, years later. Pip, now grown and the Door's new Keeper, tends the garden Tamsin planted where the fortress stood, and tells the story to children born free: of a woman who hid so long she forgot she was a door herself. Tamsin, half-wild, visits at the turning of seasons. The beat is peace earned, identity chosen, and the price paid remembered with love.
